content: GLB1, also referred to as Galactosidase, beta 1, is a protein in humans encoded by the GLB1 gene. This protein functions as a beta-galactosidase enzyme, which hydrolyzes the terminal beta-galactose residues from ganglioside substrates and other glycoconjugates. Additionally, the GLB1 gene encodes an elastin-binding protein. In maize (Zea mays), the Glb1 gene encodes a storage protein known as globulin. Clinical Significance GM1-gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by a deficiency in beta-galactosidase (GLB1). Certain cases of Morquio syndrome type B have been linked to mutations in the GLB1 gene, which result in abnormal elastic fibers in affected individuals. Elastin Receptor The GLB1 gene undergoes alternative splicing, producing two distinct mRNA transcripts. The 5-kilobase transcript encodes the beta-galactosidase enzyme, which consists of 677 amino acids. The 2.0-kilobase mRNA encodes a beta-galactosidase-related protein, known as S-Gal, which is 546 amino acids long and lacks enzymatic activity. Despite its lack of enzymatic function, the S-Gal protein binds to elastin and elastin fragments generated by proteolysis. The S-Gal protein is a peripheral membrane protein that is part of the elastin receptor complex located on the cell surface. This receptor complex includes S-Gal, neuraminidase, and Cathepsin A. When elastin-derived peptides bind to the S-Gal protein, the associated neuraminidase enzyme activity is activated. This activation can alter signal transduction pathways in responding cells, involving extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) and modulating the production of matrix metallopeptidases. Elastin-derived peptides exhibit chemotactic properties for certain cell types and can influence cell cycle progression. The elastin-binding protein derived from GLB1 and the elastin receptor complex appear to indirectly regulate cell proliferation. This regulation involves the removal of sialic acid residues from extracellular and cell surface proteins, including growth factor receptors. The S-Gal protein plays a role in the normal assembly of elastin into extracellular elastic fibers. Elastin is initially synthesized as tropoelastin, which associates with S-Gal. The enzymatic activity of neuraminidase within the elastin receptor complex facilitates the release of tropoelastin molecules from the S-Gal chaperone. Cathepsin A is also essential for the proper biosynthesis of elastin.
